design_detail: Parallel three-arm randomized trial (Study 1 of a 5-year project at the University of New Mexico, Albuquerque) in 130 concerned significant others (CSOs: spouses, partners, parents and other relatives living with a person with an alcohol problem who refused treatment). CSOs were randomized by urn randomization to Al-Anon facilitation therapy (n = 45; up to 12 one-hour sessions encouraging involvement in Al-Anon), a Johnson Institute intervention (n = 40; six sessions of about 2 hours preparing a confrontational family meeting) or community reinforcement and family training, CRAFT (n = 45; up to 12 one-hour sessions teaching behaviour-change and communication skills to use at home). All arms were manual-guided with about 12 hours of therapist contact, and therapists were nested within conditions. Primary outcome: the relative's entry into treatment within 6 months (at least the 4-hour assessment and one session), tracked to 12 months; CSO functioning measured at intake, 3 and 6 months. Relatives who agreed were offered free treatment in an embedded trial (Study 2), whose drinking outcomes are reported elsewhere.
can_establish: That, in this trial of mostly women family members of people with alcohol problems who refused treatment, being assigned to CRAFT led to treatment entry far more often within 6 and 12 months than being assigned to Al-Anon facilitation or a Johnson Institute intervention, as delivered by these therapists at this site.
cannot_establish: Whether CRAFT changes drinking or other outcomes for the relative (reported elsewhere); whether family members benefit from any of the three approaches compared with no help (all three groups improved equally and there was no untreated group); whether the advantage holds with other therapists, sites or drugs, for family members in less frequent contact, or where there is violence (excluded); or which parts of CRAFT do the work (skill use was not measured).

sample.recruitment: Community volunteers: CSOs seeking advice or help about the drinking of someone living with them, referred from various sources but mostly through announcements in local news media, living within 60 miles of the research site in Albuquerque, New Mexico (p. 688; p. 690).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: CSO living with a relative with a drinking problem who was a close relative (parent, child, grandchild, sibling), spouse or unmarried partner; contact on at least 40% of the past 90 days with no planned separation; both aged 18 or older; the relative described by the CSO, in a structured diagnostic interview (SCID), as meeting DSM-III-R criteria for alcohol abuse or dependence, refusing treatment, and untreated (other than detoxification) in the past 3 months. Excluded: CSO with a substance use disorder; unremitted psychosis or other severe psychiatric condition in either person; CSO planning more than 6 hours of other treatment in the next 3 months; relative with an illicit drug problem more severe than the alcohol problem, or any crack cocaine or injecting drug use; a Johnson intervention in the past 3 years; insufficient reading ability; relative with domestic violence or criminal assault in the past 2 years or a history of severe violence (p. 690). 50 cases excluded at screening: insufficient contact 17, the relative's violence 11, relative had not refused treatment 10, CSO unwilling 4, CSO alcohol dependent 3, relative with severe psychiatric disorder 3, relative not clearly meeting criteria 2 (p. 690).
sample.demographics: CSOs: 118 of 130 (91%) women; Hispanic 39%, White non-Hispanic 53%, Native American 6% (8), 1 African American, 1 other; age 21–81, mean 47; mean 14 years of education; 17% of family incomes below $15,000 and 53% below $30,000. Relationship to the relative: spouse 59%, parent 30%, boyfriend or girlfriend 8%, child 1.5%, grandparent 1.5%; mean relationship length 22 years (1–57); 58% had previously sought help through Al-Anon (p. 692). The relatives' own demographics are not reported.
sample.attrition: All 130 randomized CSOs were retained in the analyses (intention to treat, p. 692). Follow-up interviews: Al-Anon facilitation 44 of 45 at 3 and 6 months and 42 at 9 and 12; CRAFT 45 of 45 at 3, 6 and 9 months and 44 at 12; Johnson 39 of 40 at 3 and 6 months, 38 at 9 and 36 at 12; 94% of CSOs completed all four follow-ups (p. 693). The logistic regression used 120 CSOs with complete data (p. 694). The CSO-functioning analyses do not state their n; their error degrees of freedom (196 to 222) imply roughly 100 to 115 CSOs per measure (editors' inference).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers answering media announcements, nearly all women, in one US city with a large Hispanic population. CSOs had to see the relative on at least 40% of days, and relatives with recent violence, injecting or crack cocaine use, or a more severe drug problem were excluded. The number of callers screened by telephone is not reported. The results concern family members of people with alcohol problems, not other drugs, and not families affected by violence.

exposure.measurement: Assigned intervention (randomized). Al-Anon facilitation: up to 12 sessions of 60 minutes (8 core), adapted from Project MATCH twelve-step facilitation, delivered by four counsellors with a mean of 14 years' twelve-step experience. Johnson Institute intervention: six sessions of about 2 hours (four preparatory sessions, the confrontation meeting with the relative, one review session), delivered by two counsellors with 27 and 17 years' experience from the local council on alcoholism, supervised by a psychiatrist experienced in the method. CRAFT: up to 12 one-hour individual sessions (awareness training, contingency management, communication skills, competing activities, outside activities, handling dangerous situations, suggesting counselling, functional analysis), delivered by five less experienced therapists (four with 0–3 years, one with 6 years) using a manual by R. J. Meyers, who developed the approach and supervised the condition (pp. 691–692). Weekly supervision and videotaped sessions, with randomly selected tapes reviewed for adherence; tapes were not coded for analysis (p. 692).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Sessions attended: Al-Anon facilitation 11.4 of 12 (95%), CRAFT 10.7 of 12 (89%), Johnson 3.18 of 6 two-hour sessions (53%), because 70% of Johnson-arm CSOs chose not to hold the confrontation (p. 692).
exposure.polysubstance: Relatives with a more severe illicit drug problem, or any crack cocaine or injecting drug use, were excluded, as were CSOs with their own substance use disorder (p. 690). The relatives' other drug use is not reported in this paper.

comparison.controls: Two active comparators: Al-Anon facilitation therapy, which the authors treat as a functional no-treatment control for engagement because changing the drinker is not an Al-Anon goal (p. 688), and the Johnson Institute confrontational intervention. No waiting-list or untreated group.
comparison.matching: Urn randomization balanced CSO gender, ethnicity, education, age, relationship type, lifetime DrInC score and lifetime Al-Anon meetings; 22 baseline comparisons (16 ANOVAs, 6 chi-squares) showed no significant differences, nor did CSO estimates of drinking, consequences or the relative's motivation (pp. 691–692).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not a concern for the randomized comparison. The relatives' characteristics were known only through CSO report.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: the relative engaged in treatment within 6 months, defined as completing the initial 4-hour assessment and at least one session in the project's free treatment (Study 2), or at least two sessions of other treatment; tracked to 12 months (p. 693). CSO functioning: Beck Depression Inventory, State-Trait Anger Expression Inventory, Family Environment Scale (cohesion, conflict), Relationship Happiness Scale, at intake, 3 and 6 months (p. 694). Also collected at intake: State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, self-esteem, physical symptoms, Spouse Enabling and Sobriety Influence Inventories, Form 90, DrInC, Alcohol Dependence Scale, Dyadic Adjustment Scale and Conflict Tactics Scale (pp. 690–691).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments. Drinking data for relatives who did not enter treatment came only from CSOs; the 40% contact threshold was chosen because collateral and self-reports agreed only with frequent contact (r = .84 vs −.20 in Project MATCH data) (p. 691).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Engaged' is a low threshold (assessment plus one session); relatives who entered treatment stayed a median of 10.5 sessions (p. 693).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The primary outcome (engagement) was tested for Study 2 entry, the 6-month window and 12 months, each with a three-group test and two pairwise tests described as post hoc; five CSO measures (six F tests, state and trait anger separately) in one repeated-measures model.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Follow-up interviews by independent research staff unaware of group assignment and of clinical procedures (p. 692). CSOs and therapists could not be blind. Entry into Study 2 treatment was recorded by the project; entry into other treatment came from CSO report.

analysis.effect_sizes: Engaged within 6 months (primary): CRAFT 29/45 (64%), Johnson 12/40 (30%), Al-Anon facilitation 6/45 (13%); χ²(2, N = 130) = 27.33, p < .0001; CRAFT vs Johnson χ²(1, N = 85) = 10.29, p < .001 (Table 1; p. 693). Editors' calculation (Wald intervals): risk difference CRAFT minus Johnson 34 percentage points (95% CI about 14 to 54), CRAFT minus Al-Anon facilitation 51 points (34 to 68); about 3 and 2 families, respectively, trained in CRAFT for each additional relative engaged. Within 12 months: 67%, 35% and 20% (Table 1). Al-Anon facilitation vs Johnson not significant (6 months χ²(1, N = 85) = 3.56, p < .06). Condition remained associated with engagement after adjustment for drinking at intake, extra CSO therapy and relationship type: Wald χ²(2, N = 120) = 17.27, p < .0002 (p. 694). CSO functioning: no group × time interactions and no group main effects; time effects for depression F(2, 196) = 14.49, state anger F(2, 222) = 10.65, trait anger F(2, 214) = 8.48, family conflict F(2, 206) = 10.28, family cohesion F(2, 204) = 10.59, relationship happiness F(2, 198) = 9.00 (p. 694; Table 2).
analysis.covariates: Primary comparison unadjusted (chi-square tests, which the editors' recalculation shows are likelihood-ratio statistics). Logistic regression adjusted for the CSO-reported percentage of days abstinent at intake, the number of additional therapy sessions in months 1–3, and relationship type (p. 694). CSO outcomes adjusted for therapy received outside the project (p. 694).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration (published 1999) and no protocol cited; the primary outcome, engagement within 6 months, is named in the Results (p. 693).
analysis.selective_reporting: Drinking outcomes of the relatives are deferred to a later report of Study 2 (p. 696). Several intake measures (anxiety, self-esteem, physical symptoms, enabling, Dyadic Adjustment Scale, Conflict Tactics Scale) are not reported as outcomes.
analysis.power: Not reported. The CRAFT difference was large enough for this sample; the Al-Anon facilitation vs Johnson comparison (13% vs 30%) was not clearly resolved (p < .06).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Family members trained in CRAFT got their relative into treatment within 6 months in 64% of cases, against 30% after the Johnson intervention and 13% after Al-Anon facilitation; at 12 months the figures were 67%, 35% and 20%. In the Johnson arm 70% of families did not hold the confrontation; of the 12 that did, 9 relatives entered treatment. Family members in all three arms reported less depression, anger and family conflict and more cohesion and relationship happiness over 6 months, to the same degree, whether or not the relative entered treatment. Parents engaged the relative more often than spouses (51% vs 32% at 6 months).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's and discussion's central claim, that CRAFT was more effective at engaging relatives in treatment, matches the results, and the discussion is careful that Al-Anon facilitation is not the same as a simple referral to Al-Anon and that no single trial is conclusive (pp. 695–696). Gaps: (1) the abstract says all three approaches were associated with similar improvement for family members; with no untreated group, that improvement cannot be credited to any of the interventions (time, regression to the mean and the act of seeking help are alternatives); (2) the discussion calls the Johnson and Al-Anon approaches 'comparatively ineffective' at starting treatment and says a majority of unmotivated relatives can be engaged through the family (p. 696), on the evidence of one site and one team, with therapists nested within conditions and the CRAFT condition supervised by its developer, a co-author; (3) 'more effective' refers to treatment entry only, not to drinking or wellbeing outcomes, which this report does not give.

timeline.event: Sisson and Azrin: 12 CSOs; 6 of 7 relatives entered treatment after community reinforcement training against none after an Al-Anon approach delivered by the same behaviour therapists, which the present authors call an unfair comparison (as described, p. 689).
Thomas et al.: unilateral family therapy with spouses; 8 of 13 treated cases (62%) entered treatment or cut drinking substantially (as described, pp. 689, 695).
This trial: CRAFT 64% vs Johnson 30% vs Al-Anon facilitation 13% engaged within 6 months.
Same group, CRAFT with CSOs of people who used illicit drugs: 74% engaged (Meyers, Miller, Hill & Tonigan, described as in press, p. 695; an uncontrolled study by the account of Roozen et al., 2010).
Meta-analysis of four RCTs including this one: CRAFT vs Al-Anon/Nar-Anon RR 3.25 (2.11–5.02); vs Johnson, this trial alone, RR 2.15

replication.where_it_stands: The engagement advantage of CRAFT over twelve-step family approaches was repeated in two later RCTs with families of people who use illicit drugs (Kirby et al., 1999; Meyers et al., 2002, as summarized by Roozen et al., 2010), one of them from the same group; the comparison with the Johnson intervention rests on this trial alone. No trial in this set had an untreated control for family members' wellbeing.

funding.funder: Supported in part by Grant R01-AA09774 from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (author note, p. 688).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: R. J. Meyers, second and corresponding author, originally developed the approach that CRAFT extends, wrote the CRAFT manual and supervised the CRAFT condition (pp. 691–692). The authors nested therapists within conditions so that each approach was delivered by therapists committed to it (p. 692). Investigator allegiance is recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A multi-site randomized trial run by teams independent of CRAFT's developers, with several therapists per condition (or therapists crossed with conditions), including family members of people who use drugs other than alcohol and those in less frequent contact, comparing CRAFT with usual care or a waiting list, and measuring treatment entry, the relative's substance use and safety, and family members' wellbeing for at least 12 months.

domains.domain: Bias arising from the randomization process
domains.note: Urn randomization balancing seven variables, and 22 baseline comparisons showed no differences; how allocation was concealed from the staff enrolling CSOs is not described.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Effect of assignment, analysed by intention to treat (all 130). CSOs and therapists knew the assignment, unavoidably; adherence was supervised by videotape. Not holding the confrontation (70%) is part of the Johnson approach as offered. Outside RoB 2's questions: therapists were nested within conditions, with less experienced therapists in CRAFT supervised by its developer, so method and therapist team cannot be separated (the two main CRAFT therapists engaged 50% and 91%).

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: Engagement status is known for all randomized CSOs, and 94% completed all follow-ups. (For the CSO-functioning outcomes, the analyses' degrees of freedom imply about 12% to 23% missing, editors' inference.)

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Entry into the project's treatment was recorded by the project; other treatment was reported by CSOs to interviewers unaware of assignment. (The CSO-functioning outcomes are self-reports by participants who knew their assignment.)

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registered protocol or analysis plan. Engagement is reported for three windows with three-group and post hoc pairwise tests, all in the same direction; the relatives' drinking outcomes are deferred to a later report.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Judged for the primary outcome, treatment entry. A well-conducted trial for its time: randomized with balance checks, intention to treat, follow-up interviewers unaware of assignment and 94% retention. The concerns (allocation concealment not described, no registered plan) are unlikely to explain a 34-point difference, but the comparison is of three therapist teams at one site, one led by the method's developer, which limits how far the size of the effect generalizes. For family members' own wellbeing the trial shows only equal improvement in all arms, without an untreated comparison, so it cannot show that any approach caused it. Citable for: CRAFT's advantage in getting relatives with alcohol problems into treatment over Al-Anon facilitation and the Johnson intervention; the Johnson intervention's 70% non-completion; not for drinking outcomes or for benefits to family members.

key_findings.finding: Who was studied: 130 family members (91% women; spouses 59%, parents 30%, partners 8%) living with a relative with an alcohol problem who refused treatment, in Albuquerque, New Mexico; randomized to Al-Anon facilitation (45), the Johnson Institute intervention (40) or CRAFT (45), and all retained in the analysis.

Within 6 months (primary outcome), the relative entered treatment in 29 of 45 CRAFT cases (64%), 12 of 40 Johnson cases (30%) and 6 of 45 Al-Anon facilitation cases (13%); χ²(2, N = 130) = 27.33, p < .0001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Engagement, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (Wald intervals): CRAFT minus Johnson 34 percentage points (95% CI about 14 to 54); CRAFT minus Al-Anon facilitation 51 points (34 to 68).

key_findings.finding: Within 12 months, engagement was 67% with CRAFT, 35% with the Johnson intervention and 20% with Al-Anon facilitation (χ²(2, N = 130) = 23.78, p < .0001); 74% of the relatives who entered treatment in the year had done so by the end of the family member's counselling (3 months) and 90% by 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Engagement, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: The Al-Anon 12-month figure is inconsistent within the paper (20% in Table 1, about 18% implied by the text and the test statistic); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: CRAFT also beat the Johnson intervention alone: χ²(1, N = 85) = 15.66 for Study 2 entry, 10.29 at 6 months (p < .001) and 8.65 at 12 months (p < .003); Al-Anon facilitation and the Johnson intervention did not differ significantly (χ² 1.23, 3.56 and 3.29).

In the Johnson arm, 70% of family members decided not to go through with the confrontation. Of the 12 families that held it, 9 relatives (75%) entered treatment, all within 6 months; of the 28 that did not, 3 (11%) entered within 6 months and 5 (18%) within 12 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › CSO Participation, 1st paragraph (p. 692); Treatment Engagement, 4th paragraph (p. 693)

key_findings.finding: Timing: median 47 days from the family member's first session to the relative's first treatment session; family members had completed a mean of 4.7 CRAFT sessions (median 4), 5.7 Al-Anon facilitation sessions (median 6) or 4.7 Johnson sessions (median 6) before the relative entered treatment; relatives who entered stayed a median of 10.5 sessions.

Condition remained a significant predictor of engagement after adjusting for drinking at intake, extra therapy for the family member and relationship type (Wald χ²(2, N = 120) = 17.27, p < .0002). Relationship type also predicted engagement: across conditions, parents engaged the relative more often than spouses (51% vs 32% at 6 months; 56% vs 34% at 12 months).
key_findings.locator: Results › Treatment Engagement, 6th paragraph (begins p. 693, continues p. 694)

key_findings.finding: Family members' own functioning improved over 6 months by similar amounts in all three arms, with no group × time interaction and no group effect: for example, Beck Depression Inventory means fell from 10.6–10.8 at intake to 7.0–7.5 at 6 months, and family conflict, anger, cohesion and relationship happiness changed in the same direction (time effects p < .001 to p < .002). Improvement did not depend on whether the relative entered treatment.
key_findings.locator: Results › CSO Improvement, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 2
key_findings.note: There was no untreated group, so the improvement cannot be attributed to any of the three approaches. Table 2 gives no n per cell.

key_findings.finding: Attendance: family members completed 11.4 of 12 Al-Anon facilitation sessions (95%), 10.7 of 12 CRAFT sessions (89%) and 3.18 of 6 Johnson sessions (53%). In the 90 days after randomization, 75% in the Al-Anon facilitation arm attended Al-Anon against 18% in each other arm (N = 109), and they received more outside therapy sessions (mean 4.81 vs 2.03 and 2.62).
key_findings.locator: Results › CSO Participation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (2nd begins p. 692, continues p. 693)

key_findings.finding: Therapist differences: engagement rates per therapist ranged from 16% to 100% across the 11 therapists, and the lowest CRAFT therapist (50%) exceeded the highest in the other arms; the two CRAFT therapists with 10 or more cases differed (7/14, 50%, vs 10/11, 91%; χ²(1, N = 25) = 5.23, p < .02), whereas the pairs in the other arms did not (16% and 17%; 33% and 36%). CRAFT therapists had less experience than those in the other arms.
key_findings.locator: Method › Therapists, 2nd paragraph (p. 692); Results › Therapist Differences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3 (p. 695)

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the Al-Anon facilitation tested here, a structured 12-session individual therapy, cannot be equated with a simple referral to Al-Anon; that no trial, including this one, documented whether family members actually learned and used the skills taught; and that the 40% contact requirement leaves open whether less frequent contact would give similar results.

reporting_issues.issue: The Al-Anon facilitation arm's 12-month engagement is inconsistent. Tables 1 and 3 give 9 of 45 relatives engaged by 12 months (20%), with 6 later engagements across arms (3, 2 and 1), but the text says 5 additional clients entered treatment in months 7–12. By the editors' recalculation, all nine reported chi-squares are likelihood-ratio statistics that reproduce from the Table 1 counts, except the two 12-month tests involving the Al-Anon arm (23.78 and 3.29), which reproduce only with 8 of 45 engaged (with 9 of 45 they would be 21.64 and 2.42). The statement that 90% of relatives were engaged by 6 months also fits 47 of 52 (90.4%) better than 47 of 53 (88.7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Al-Anon facilitation 12-month rate was probably 18% (8 of 45) rather than 20%; the conclusions are unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: The 12-month comparison of Al-Anon facilitation with the Johnson intervention is printed as χ²(2, N = 85) = 3.29, with 2 degrees of freedom for a two-group comparison; the printed p < .07 corresponds to 1 degree of freedom.

The report says all randomized CSOs were retained for all analyses (intention to treat), but the F tests for the CSO-functioning measures have error degrees of freedom from 196 to 222, which by the editors' inference for a three-group repeated-measures model with one covariate implies roughly 100 to 115 CSOs per measure; Table 2 gives no n.
reporting_issues.consequence: The family-member outcomes may rest on 77% to 88% of the randomized sample, and the meta-analysis that pooled them (Roozen et al., 2010) used n = 45 for the CRAFT arm at both times.
